analysis.one_liner: Restores the FTC's power to make companies that defraud consumers hand back the money.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 221-205 in July 2021, but the Senate never voted on it, and the bill died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In April 2021 the Supreme Court ruled that the FTC could no longer go to court and win refunds, restitution, or disgorgement of profits from companies that ran scams or false ads. This bill wrote that power back into law, letting the FTC recover money for cheated consumers. The House passed it on July 20, 2021, on a near party-line vote, but the Senate never brought it up, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who were cheated by false advertising, fraud, or anticompetitive practices, because the FTC could again sue in federal court to recover their losses, cancel unfair contracts, refund money, return property, and force companies to give up profits made from wrongdoing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers cheated by scams and false ads

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes the FTC to seek monetary relief in federal court from businesses that engage in unlawful commercial practices such as false advertising, consumer fraud, and anticompetitive conduct.
Lets the FTC seek restitution for losses, rescission or reformation of contracts, refunds of money, return of property, and disgorgement of unjust enrichment.
Restores the authority the Supreme Court eliminated on April 22, 2021, in AMG Capital Management, LLC v. FTC, when it held the FTC Act does not authorize the FTC to seek such relief.

analysis.who_pays: Companies found to have engaged in fraud, false advertising, or anticompetitive conduct, which could be ordered to repay victims or hand over profits gained from the violation; the bill applies a 10-year lookback limit on such claims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies sued for fraud and false ads

drawbacks.text: The bill applies to violations of any provision of law the FTC enforces, a broad grant, and applies to actions pending at enactment, so companies could face court-ordered repayment for conduct long past.

Supporters of the Supreme Court's ruling argued the FTC had been using an ambiguous statutory provision to extract monetary penalties in administrative cases without full court process; writing the power into law restores an enforcement tool some businesses viewed as overreach.

The monetary relief would go through FTC lawsuits in federal court rather than directly to victims automatically, and the bill includes a 10-year limit and an offset that reduces disgorgement by any restitution paid.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside is concrete: a tool the FTC had used to win billions in refunds for scam victims was taken away by a court ruling and this bill restored it. The cost falls on companies that violate consumer protection laws, though some businesses faced added legal uncertainty over how far back the FTC could reach. The main weakness is not the design but the fate: the Senate never considered it.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 221-205 on July 20, 2021, but the Senate received it the next day and never voted, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced April 20, 2021, and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees.
The Energy and Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported as amended by a 30-22 vote on June 10, 2021, and reported it on July 16, 2021, after the Judiciary Committee was discharged.
On July 20, 2021, the House rejected a Republican motion to recommit the bill 207-217, with all 217 voting Democrats opposed and all 207 voting Republicans in favor.
The House passed the bill 221-205 that same day, with 219 of 219 voting Democrats in favor and only 2 of 211 voting Republicans in favor.
The Senate received the bill on July 21, 2021, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress, so it died without a vote on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that defraud or mislead consumers are better off, because the FTC's power to recover refunds and disgorged profits from them stayed off the books. The Supreme Court's AMG ruling limiting the FTC also remains the operative law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies that defraud or mislead consumers

for.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill as amended, 30-22, on July 16, 2021.

against.name: 205 of 211 voting House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against final passage, 205-2, and backed the failed motion to recommit the bill to committee.

against.name: Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a Senate floor vote after the House passed it.

sides.party_line_note: The final House vote split almost entirely by party: 219 of 219 voting Democrats voted yes, while only 2 of 211 voting Republicans joined them.

industries.industry: Companies engaged in false advertising, consumer fraud, and anticompetitive conduct
industries.note: The bill would have let the FTC sue them in federal court for restitution, refunds, and disgorgement of profits, reopening a recovery tool the Supreme Court shut off in April 2021. Its failure means consumers cheated in those cases cannot get that money back through the FTC.
FTC enforcement attorneys and the private plaintiffs' bar would gain a large new avenue of restitution and disgorgement cases; the bill's death keeps that work off the docket.
